897.title: Herod's Temple
897.hook: a hard king rebuilds the Temple, and one of its great outer walls still stands
897.howItsDone: Jews pray at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, and visitors leave folded written prayers in the cracks between its stones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, genizah: old words found again in caves near the Dead Sea. Your line was hidden in caves. Today, a new part opens: Rome, destruction, and the rabbis.

Folded slips of paper, pushed into the cracks between huge pale stones. Small green plants growing out of the joints. Some press their foreheads to the stone; some read psalms; some just lay a hand flat on the wall and stay. This is the Western Wall in Jerusalem, in Hebrew the Kotel. It isn't the Temple itself. It's part of the great outer wall that held up the platform the Temple once stood on. Why pray at a retaining wall? Go back to the man who built it: Herod.
screen: `PAPERS IN THE CRACKS.` → `NOT THE TEMPLE, BUT ITS WALL.` → `GO BACK TO HEROD.`

segments.voice: Herod was a king of Judea who ruled with Rome's backing. The Jewish historian Josephus tells his story, and it isn't gentle: Josephus records a suspicious, violent king who had members of his own family put to death. And he set out to rebuild the Second Temple, the house that had stood since the return from Babylon. Josephus describes the hill enlarged, enormous walls raised to hold up a wide, level court, and a sanctuary so covered in gold and white stone that from far off it looked like a snowy mountain. The rabbis tell a harder story about how it began. In tractate Bava Batra, Herod has killed the sages. One survives, Bava ben Buta, whom Herod has blinded. Herod, in disguise, tries to trick him into cursing the king. He won't. Herod asks how he could make amends, and the sage answers, in paraphrase: you darkened the light of the world, so go and tend the light of the world. Rebuild the Temple. The same page keeps a saying, in paraphrase: whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building. The rabbis keep the cruelty and the beauty, and smooth over neither. The sanctuary would not last, but part of the western retaining wall did. One midrash reads a line from the Song of Songs, "behold, he standeth behind our wall", and says God's presence never leaves the Western Wall. The Hebrew word for wall in that verse is the same word people use for the Kotel.
screen: `A HARD KING REBUILDS THE TEMPLE.` · `A BLINDED SAGE SAYS: TEND THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `NEVER SEEN A BEAUTIFUL BUILDING.` · then: `"BEHIND OUR WALL."`

segments.voice: Hold the scene in your mind, or find a picture of the Western Wall, and pick one stone to stay with; someone cut it for Herod, and many hands have touched it since. Then think of one thing in your life that outlasted something larger, like a recipe that outlived a kitchen. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know, the way people do at the wall.
Herod's Temple. Rebuilt by a hard king, praised even by the rabbis who remembered his cruelty, and part of its western wall still stands.
Your line: the wall remains. A cruel king, and a beautiful house. Day eight hundred ninety-seven, done.

898.title: Two schools
898.hook: the houses of Hillel and Shammai argue, and the Talmud keeps both sides
898.howItsDone: Jewish study often happens in pairs, and the Talmud records minority opinions, including those of the house of Shammai, alongside the law that was followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's Temple, and a wall still standing. Your line was the wall remains. Today, two teachers and the schools that grew around them.

Who gets to be right when two serious people disagree? A man comes to a teacher named Shammai with a challenge: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai, the Talmud says, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. He goes to Hillel and asks the same thing. Hillel answers, in paraphrase: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it. Two teachers, two temperaments, and around them grew two schools whose arguments fill page after page of the rabbis' writings.
screen: `THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT?` → `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` → `HILLEL: GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai. A house here means a school: the students, and their students after them. They disagreed about real things: which blessing comes first on a Friday night, how to light the Hanukkah lamps, whether you must lie down to say the evening Shema. The house of Shammai often takes the stricter side, but the Mishnah keeps a list of cases where it's the other way. Then the famous passage, in tractate Eruvin. The two houses argued for three years, each saying the law follows us. Finally a voice from heaven spoke, in paraphrase: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. So why Hillel? The Talmud's answer isn't that they were smarter. It's that they were gentle and patient. They taught their own view and the view of the house of Shammai, and even mentioned Shammai's view before their own. The law went to the people who listened best. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, adds a postscript: an argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. The losing side isn't erased. Its words are still printed and studied, and some readers say keeping them is a kind of respect: the minority view sits on the page beside the majority, for anyone who comes later.

segments.voice: Choose one person who sees something very differently than you do: faith, politics, how to load a dishwasher. Try the house of Hillel's habit: say their view to yourself first, as fairly as you can, in words they'd recognize, then say your own, and notice what changes. You don't have to agree; if you pray, you can hold them in that prayer by name.
Two schools. The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, whose arguments the Talmud keeps side by side, and whose law goes to the house that listened.
Your line: the house of hillel. Both sides stay on the page. See you tomorrow.

899.title: The Great Revolt (66–70 CE)
899.hook: a revolt against Rome ends with Jerusalem and the Temple burned
899.howItsDone: Jews mark the fall of both Temples on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, with a fast, by sitting low like mourners, and by reading the book of Lamentations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two schools, both called the words of the living God. Your line was the house of hillel. Today, their city goes up in flames.

A man in Jerusalem throws a party and tells his servant to invite his friend Kamtza. The servant brings Bar Kamtza instead, a man the host can't stand. The host orders him out. Bar Kamtza begs: let me stay, I'll pay for what I eat. Half the feast. The whole feast. No. He is thrown out in front of everyone, and the rabbis at the table say nothing. That's how the Talmud begins its story of the fall of Jerusalem. Not with armies. With a guest list.
screen: `THE WRONG GUEST.` → `THROWN OUT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `THE RABBIS SAY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The history comes mainly through Josephus, a Jewish commander in the war who later wrote its story under Roman patronage. Judea was ruled by Rome, the governors were harsh, and the people were split among themselves. Revolt broke out, and Rome sent its legions. Inside Jerusalem, rival Jewish factions fought one another even under siege, and Josephus describes the famine inside the walls in harrowing detail. In the end the Romans broke through, and the Temple, Herod's beautiful house, burned. The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, remembers the day: the ninth of Av, the same date tradition gives for the fall of the First Temple. Then the rabbis asked why. In the Talmud's story, the humiliated Bar Kamtza goes to the Roman authorities and stirs up suspicion against Jerusalem. When the rabbis might have stopped the plot, one rabbi's overcareful scruples held them back; the Talmud says that rabbi's humility destroyed the house and burned the sanctuary. And in tractate Yoma, the rabbis say the Second Temple was destroyed because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred: people hating one another for nothing. Rome lit the fire, and the rabbis didn't deny it. But they turned the question inward, toward how people treated each other at the table. Lamentations, read on the ninth of Av, opens with the grief of an empty city: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" The day is still kept with a fast, with mourners sitting low, and with those words read aloud.
screen: `JUDEA REVOLTS AGAINST ROME.` · `THE CITY FIGHTS ITSELF UNDER SIEGE.` · then, large: `THE TEMPLE BURNS ON THE NINTH OF AV.` · then: `THE RABBIS ASK WHY: BASELESS HATRED.`

segments.voice: Sit low if you can, on a cushion or the floor, the way mourners sit on the ninth of Av, and let one loss come to mind, big or small: a person, a place, a version of your life that ended. Don't try to fix it or explain it; just let it be in the room with you. If you pray, you can say the line from Lamentations: how doth the city sit solitary.
Sinat chinam. Baseless hatred, the sin the rabbis of the Talmud blamed for the Second Temple's fall: hatred between people for nothing.
Your line: the second temple fell. The rabbis looked inward, not only at Rome. Day eight hundred ninety-nine, in the books.

900.title: Masada
900.hook: the last stronghold falls, and what it means is still argued
900.carry: all looking at the same rock
900.howItsDone: Masada is visited as a historical site in Israel; Jewish readers, teachers and historians continue to debate what its story, known from Josephus, should mean.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sinat chinam, the baseless hatred the rabbis named for the Temple's fall. Your line was the second temple fell. Today, the war's last chapter, on a rock in the desert.

A flat-topped mountain rises out of the desert near the Dead Sea, with cliffs on every side. Herod had built a palace fortress on top, with storerooms and cisterns cut into the rock. Jewish rebels had seized it early in the war, and after Jerusalem fell they still held it. Rome camped below and built a great ramp up the side of the mountain so their siege engines could reach the wall. The place is Masada. What happened at the top is still argued over, and the story comes to us through one writer.
screen: `A ROCK IN THE DESERT.` → `REBELS HOLD HEROD'S FORTRESS.` → `ROME BUILDS A RAMP.`

segments.voice: That writer is Josephus, in the last book of his Jewish War. When the Romans breach the wall and the end is certain, he says, the rebels' leader, Eleazar ben Yair, gathers the defenders and, in two long speeches, urges them to choose death for themselves and their families rather than be enslaved. Josephus says the men killed their own families, then each other by lot, and the last man killed himself. When the Romans break in the next morning, ready for battle, they find silence. A few women and children hid and survived, Josephus says, and it was from them the story became known. Then the argument. For some readers, Masada stands for courage: people who would not be slaves. For others it raises hard questions; they point to the weight Jewish law gives to every life, including one's own, and ask whether this was heroism or tragedy. Historians ask how much of the story, and of those speeches, is Josephus's own telling, written in Rome after the war, about a group he describes elsewhere in harsh terms. And some point out that the Masada story isn't one the rabbis tell; it reaches us from Josephus. All these readers are looking at the same rock. The tradition doesn't hand us one tidy meaning. It hands us one writer's account, and readers who still argue over it.
screen: `JOSEPHUS TELLS THE STORY.` · then, large: `THEY WOULD NOT BE SLAVES.` · `COURAGE, OR TRAGEDY?` · then: `HOW MUCH IS JOSEPHUS?`

segments.voice: Choose one story from your family, your town or your own past that different people tell differently. Hold the version you usually tell, then set it gently to one side and hold another, the way someone else might tell it, without picking a winner. If you pray, you can bring that story and the people in it to God without settling it.
Masada. Herod's desert fortress, the rebels' last stand against Rome, told by Josephus, and argued about ever since: courage, tragedy, or a story shaped by its teller.

901.title: From Temple to study
901.hook: at Yavneh, Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuilds Jewish life around study and prayer
901.howItsDone: Jewish prayer services follow a daily rhythm that the Talmud connects to the Temple offerings, and Torah study, in a synagogue, a study hall or at home, is itself treated as a form of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masada: a fortress on a desert rock, and a story still argued over. Your line was all looking at the same rock. Today, back in besieged Jerusalem, a teacher gets out in a coffin.

The coffin is carried to the city gate by two students, one at the head and one at the feet. The guards want to stab it, to be sure the body is dead. The students talk them out of it. Inside the coffin is their teacher, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, very much alive. That's how the Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells his escape from the besieged city. He has pretended to be sick, then pretended to die, because the zealots holding Jerusalem won't let anyone leave. Once outside, he walks to the Roman commander's tent with one request.
screen: `A COFFIN AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE TEACHER INSIDE IS ALIVE.` → `HE WALKS TO THE ROMAN TENT.`

segments.voice: In the Talmud's story the Roman is Vespasian, soon to become emperor, and he tells the rabbi to ask him for something. Among his requests, Rabbi Yochanan asks, in paraphrase: give me Yavneh and its sages. Not Jerusalem. Not the Temple. A place to keep teaching. The Talmud doesn't pretend everyone agreed. It records a sharp objection, that he should have asked Rome to spare Jerusalem itself, and it gives his reasoning: ask for that much, and he might not get even a little rescue. Think what had just been lost. Jewish worship had a center: one house, one altar, priests, offerings. With the Temple burned, what could take its place? At Yavneh, tradition says, the sages began to answer: study of Torah, and prayer. The Talmud links the daily prayers to the daily Temple offerings, so the words a person says stand where the offering once stood. Long before, the prophet Hosea had pointed this way: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." The same verse ends with an offering of a new kind; in the Hebrew, it is bulls of our lips. Words, in place of bulls. A sanctuary made of time and speech, which can be carried anywhere. In the rabbis' telling, that move, from Temple to study, is how a people without a Temple kept going. The house was gone. The conversation went on.
screen: `GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `SOME SAID HE SHOULD HAVE ASKED MORE.` · then, large: `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · then: `A SANCTUARY YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: Choose something that changed and can't go back to the way it was: a job, a home, a friendship, a way your body used to work. Then ask Rabbi Yochanan's question, not how do I get the whole city back, but what is my Yavneh: one small thing I can still build, here, that carries what mattered. If you pray, you can take with you words, as Hosea says, and return.
Yavneh. The town Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asked Rome for, where Jewish life was rebuilt around Torah study and prayer after the Temple fell.
Your line: words, in place of bulls. The teaching found a new home. Nine hundred one days now.

902.title: The table is the altar (Berakhot 55a)
902.hook: the Talmud says that now a person's table atones, through hospitality
902.howItsDone: In Jewish homes that keep the custom, the bread blessed at the start of a meal is touched to salt, a custom linked to the salted Temple offerings, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is counted a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yavneh, where words took the place of offerings. Your line was words, in place of bulls. Today, the rabbis find an altar somewhere unexpected.

A plate of bread, a small dish of salt. At some Jewish tables, before the meal, someone says the blessing over the bread, breaks it, and touches each piece to the salt before passing it around. It looks like a simple kitchen habit. Tradition ties it to a memory: in the Torah, the offerings brought to the altar were salted. "With all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt." The altar is gone. The salt is still on the table. And the Talmud has a line about where the altar went.
screen: `BREAD AND A DISH OF SALT.` → `THE OFFERINGS WERE SALTED.` → `WHERE DID THE ALTAR GO?`

segments.voice: It's in tractate Berakhot, page fifty-five. The passage lists things that lengthen a person's days, and one is lingering long at your table. Why? Because a poor person might come, and you'll be there to feed them. Then two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, both say, in paraphrase: as long as the Temple stood, the altar atoned for Israel; now that it's gone, a person's table atones for them. The rabbis anchor this in a verse from Ezekiel's vision of the future Temple. The verse begins by describing an altar of wood, and in the same breath calls it a table: "This is the table that is before the LORD." It starts as an altar and ends as a table. The commentator Rashi explains how a table atones: through hospitality, by feeding guests and the hungry. So the rabbis took the altar, the center of the old worship, and set it down in the kitchen. At Yavneh, words stood in for offerings. Here, a meal does. The house of God is gone, so every house gets a piece of its work. The measure of a table isn't the food on it. It's who has a seat. A meal shared with someone who needed one becomes, in the rabbis' language, a kind of offering, and some readers hear the salt on the bread as a small reminder of that.

903.title: Bar Kokhba (132–135 CE)
903.hook: a second revolt is crushed, and Jews are barred from Jerusalem
903.howItsDone: The fall of Betar is remembered on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, alongside the destruction of both Temples, in the fast and the readings of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Berakhot, and a table that took the altar's place. Your line was it's who has a seat. Today, a second revolt against Rome, and a hope that rose very high.

"There shall step forth a star out of Jacob." That's a line from the book of Numbers, spoken by Balaam, a promise of a ruler rising from Israel. Years after the Temple burned, a new Jewish commander rose up against Rome, and Rabbi Akiva, a teacher honored by the sages, looked at him and reached for that verse. His name was Koziba, and Akiva read it into the verse: not a star, but Koziba, steps forth out of Jacob. When he saw the man, Akiva said: this is the king, the anointed one. The fighter became known as Bar Kokhba, son of a star.
screen: `"A STAR OUT OF JACOB."` → `AKIVA POINTS TO A COMMANDER.` → `SON OF A STAR.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Jerusalem Talmud, in tractate Taanit. Not everyone agreed with Akiva. Another sage, Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta, answered with a sharp, sad line, in paraphrase: Akiva, grass will grow out of your cheeks, and the son of David still won't have come. You'll be long buried before the redemption arrives, and this isn't it. The revolt was crushed. The Mishnah, in the same list of grief we met with the Temple's fall, records that on the ninth of Av the fortress of Betar was captured. Rome made Jerusalem a Roman city with a new name, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from entering it. Other rabbinic passages call the commander Bar Koziba, and some readers hear in it son of a lie, a bitter play on the same name. One man, two nicknames, and the gap between them is the story. The rabbis didn't hide that their honored teacher backed a hope that failed. They kept Akiva's words and Yochanan ben Torta's answer side by side, the way they kept Hillel and Shammai, and the page leaves a question for whoever reads it: what do you do with a hope that failed?
screen: `GRASS WILL GROW FROM YOUR CHEEKS.` · `BETAR FALLS ON THE NINTH OF AV.` · then, large: `SON OF A STAR, SON OF A LIE.` · then: `THE RABBIS KEEP THE MISTAKE.`

segments.voice: Let one hope come back to you that didn't come true: a plan, a person you trusted, a cause you were sure of. Say plainly, inside, this didn't work, with no reason and no lesson yet, and notice that you are still here, still breathing, after it. As the week closes, look back too: a wall, two schools, a fall, a fortress, a coffin, a table. If you pray, you can bring the hope that failed to God.
Bar Kokhba. Son of a star, Akiva called him; the revolt was crushed, Betar fell, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem. The rabbis kept the hope and the failure on the record.
Your line: after the revolt. Akiva's words are still there, and so is the answer that told him he was wrong. Day nine hundred three, and a week complete.
